item.title: The Charisma of the Central Limit Theorem
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
The central limit theorem (CLT) says that the average of a large enough random sample is approximately normally distributed, even when the original data is heavily skewed, uniform or U-shaped. That lets us use the normal bell curve to calculate probabilities for sample averages.

Why the CLT is so useful

  • We need not know the population shape. In practice we rarely know the true distribution of what we study. The CLT tells us the sample average behaves predictably anyway.
  • It powers statistical inference. Confidence intervals, t-tests, z-tests and A/B tests all rely on it to measure the margin of error.
  • It makes sampling practical. Instead of surveying millions of people, we can sample 1,000 and estimate the national average with a known margin of error.

Seeing it in R

Let’s draw from a strongly right-skewed population (exponential, mean 1) and look at the distribution of sample means for growing .

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(7)
sizes <- c(1, 5, 30, 100)
means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  data.frame(n = factor(paste("n =", n), levels = paste("n =", sizes)),
             mean = replicate(5000, mean(rexp(n))))
}))

ggplot(means, aes(mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ n, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean", y = "Count")

The raw data () is far from normal, yet the sample means become symmetric and bell-shaped as grows. They also get narrower, with spread :

data.frame(n = sizes,
           sd_of_means = round(as.numeric(tapply(means$mean, means$n, sd)), 3),
           theory = round(1 / sqrt(sizes), 3))
    n sd_of_means theory
1   1       0.990  1.000
2   5       0.446  0.447
3  30       0.183  0.183
4 100       0.101  0.100

When the CLT works

For the classical CLT, the sampling process should meet four conditions:

  1. Independence: each observation does not influence the next.
  2. Identical distribution: all observations come from the same population or process.
  3. Large enough : a common rule of thumb is for moderately skewed data. Symmetric data may need only about 10, and heavily skewed data or more.
  4. Finite mean and variance: must exist and .

When the CLT fails

  • Infinite variance (heavy tails). The Cauchy distribution and some Pareto distributions (financial crashes, earthquake magnitudes) have tails so heavy that larger samples never smooth out the average, since one huge outlier can wreck the mean at any time.
  • Dependent data. In time series such as daily stock prices or hourly temperatures, today depends on yesterday. Standard CLT formulas then badly underestimate the margin of error.
  • Sample too small for extreme skew. If 99.9% of users pay $0 and 0.1% pay $500, a sample of 30 is almost always all zeros. The sample averages stay skewed until is in the thousands.
  • Looking at individual points, not averages. The CLT is about sums and averages. A larger sample never makes the raw heights, incomes or waiting times look like a bell curve.
Scenario Does the CLT work? Reason
Average of dice rolls Yes Independent, finite variance,
Average of skewed incomes Yes Finite variance and a large sample
Average of Cauchy random variables No Infinite variance: the average never stabilises
Average of daily stock prices No Observations are correlated over time
Individual customer wait times () No The CLT governs averages, not raw values

Worked example: delivery times

Suppose an online store wants the true average delivery time over all 500,000 orders this year. Delivery times are right-skewed: most parcels arrive in 2 or 3 days, a few take two weeks. We sample orders and get:

Quantity Symbol Value
Sample size 100 orders
Sample mean 3.4 days
Sample standard deviation 1.5 days

Step 1: the standard error

Since is well above 30, the CLT says the sample mean is approximately normal. Its spread is the standard error:

Step 2a: a 95% confidence interval

On a normal curve, 95% of sample means fall within 1.96 standard errors of the true mean (the same idea as the 68-95-99.7 Empirical Rule, with 1.96 as the exact multiplier for 95%):

Although the raw delivery data is skewed and we checked only 100 of 500,000 orders, we can be 95% confident that the true average delivery time lies between 3.11 and 3.69 days.

Step 2b: testing a claim

Marketing wants to advertise “Average delivery in 3 days!” Is our 3.4 just sampling noise, or evidence that the true mean is worse than 3? We count how many standard errors 3.4 is above 3.0:

The one-sided probability of landing 2.67 or more standard errors above the mean by chance is about 0.0038. That is far below the usual 5% cutoff, so we reject the 3-day claim: the true average delivery time is very likely longer than 3 days.

Note

With estimated from the data, the exact reference distribution is the t-distribution. For it is almost identical to the normal, so the result is the same here.

Inference tool Formula Question answered
Standard error How much does the sample average bounce around due to luck?
Confidence interval What is a realistic range for the true average?
Hypothesis test () Is the difference real, or random noise?

Can we use it on non-normal data?

Yes. This is the main superpower of the CLT. It helps to separate two levels of data:

  • The raw data stays non-normal. If most customers spend $0 and a few spend $500, plotting 10,000 individual customers will always look skewed.
  • The sample averages become normal. Take 100 customers at a time, compute the average spend, and repeat: those averages cluster around the true mean in a symmetric bell curve, because high and low values inside each sample cancel out.

How large must be depends on the skew:

  • Mildly skewed or uniform data: about .
  • Heavily skewed data (incomes, website clicks): perhaps to .
  • Infinite variance (Cauchy): never, however large gets.
Goal Normal / CLT math OK? Why
Estimate the population mean (confidence interval) Yes The sample mean is approximately normal for large
Compare two group means (A/B test, t-test) Yes Both group means become approximately normal
Predict one individual’s value (prediction interval) No Individual values keep the original non-normal shape

Hypothesis testing on non-normal data

Standard t-tests and z-tests do not need the raw data to be bell-shaped. They need only the sample mean (or the difference of two means) to be approximately normal, which the CLT provides when the sample is large enough.

  • Large sample ( for mild skew, for heavy skew): run the standard t-test or z-test directly.
  • Small sample () with non-normal data: the CLT has not kicked in, so p-values from a t-test can mislead. Use a non-parametric test (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank) or bootstrapping.

Even with a large sample, avoid CLT-based tests in these situations:

  • We care about the median, not the mean. For skewed data such as income or house prices, the mean is pulled far from the typical value, and a test on the median is more meaningful.
  • Extreme outliers or infinite variance. The sample mean never stabilises, and t-tests lose power.
  • One tiny group in an A/B test. Both groups need enough observations. With but , the CLT assumption still breaks down for group B.
Data shape Sample size Best test
Normal Any (even ) Standard t-test
Skewed, uniform or U-shaped Large ( to 100+) Standard t-test (powered by the CLT)
Skewed, uniform or U-shaped Small () Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon test
Heavy outliers (testing medians) Any Mann-Whitney U or bootstrap test

Key takeaway

  • The CLT is about averages, not individual values.
  • It lets us do inference without knowing the population’s shape, provided the sample is large, the observations are independent and the variance is finite.
  • The more skewed the data, the larger the sample we need.

item.title: Complex Numbers: Why They Are as Real as Real Numbers, and How They Simplify Calculations
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Complex numbers are just as “real” as real numbers: both are abstract models that people created to describe the physical world. The labels “real” and “imaginary” are historical accidents, and complex numbers are essential for modelling waves, rotations and oscillations.

Why they are equally “real”

  • Both are human abstractions. We cannot hold or in our hands any more than we can hold . Each is a set of rules that reliably predicts how nature behaves.
  • An unfortunate name. In the 17th century René Descartes called these numbers “imaginary”, as a mild insult, because square roots of negative numbers troubled him. The name stuck, although the numbers are completely consistent.
  • Two-dimensional numbers. A real number sits on a line. A complex number sits on a plane, with a real part and an imaginary part . Multiplying by is a 90-degree rotation, which is as physical as moving forward or backward.

The complex plane

We draw the real part on the horizontal axis and the imaginary part on the vertical axis. So is the point 3 to the right and 2 up.

The same point can be described by its length and direction, the polar form:

Here and .

Multiplying by rotates by 90 degrees

Complex arithmetic follows the usual rules together with . For example:

Multiplying our point by turns it a quarter turn counter-clockwise, and four turns bring it back:

More generally, multiplying complex numbers multiplies their lengths and adds their angles. This one fact is behind most of the shortcuts below.

How complex numbers ease real-world calculations

Complex numbers replace messy trigonometry with simple arithmetic. Here are small examples that we can do by hand.

1. AC circuits

In alternating current, voltage and current oscillate like waves and drift out of step. Engineers give each component a complex impedance : a resistor is , an inductor is (engineers write for ). Series impedances simply add, and Ohm’s law still holds.

Take a resistor of 3 in series with an inductor of 4 (reactance), driven by 10 V:

The size of the current is A, and its angle is , so the current lags the voltage by 53 degrees. One short calculation gives both the amount and the timing. With sines and cosines we would be solving a differential equation or juggling phase-shift identities.

2. Rotating points in 2D graphics

Rotating a point by an angle normally needs the matrix

With complex numbers it is a single multiplication, . To rotate the point by 45 degrees, multiply by (since radians is exactly 45 degrees):

So moves to , straight up the imaginary axis, exactly as a 45-degree turn should. Chaining two rotations just multiplies the factors.

3. Signals and Wi-Fi

A wave needs both a cosine and a sine to describe its size and timing. The single complex number carries both at once. This is why the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), which splits a messy signal into clean frequencies, is written with complex numbers. The same idea powers Wi-Fi, streaming video and phone calls.

4. Other places

  • Quantum mechanics. Schrödinger’s equation, which governs atoms, lasers and semiconductors, contains explicitly.
  • Control systems and aviation. Engineers place a system’s behaviour on the complex plane to see whether an aircraft will settle after turbulence or spiral out of control.

Drawing a circle with complex numbers in R

The equation of a circle with centre and radius is usually written as an implicit equation:

It describes the circle but does not tell us how to plot it: plot() needs points, so we must solve for twice (upper and lower halves). In the complex plane the same circle is one compact formula, with the centre :

As runs around, walks once round the unit circle, so we get the points directly:

c0 <- 2 + 1i      # centre
r  <- 3           # radius
t  <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)

z  <- c0 + r * exp(1i * t)

ggplot(data.frame(re = Re(z), im = Im(z)), aes(re, im)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_path(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = Re(c0), y = Im(c0), colour = "tomato", size = 3) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = "Real axis", y = "Imaginary axis")
Note

With real numbers we would write x <- h + r * cos(t) and y <- k + r * sin(t) separately. Complex numbers pack both coordinates into one value, so shifting (adding ), scaling (multiplying by ) and rotating (multiplying by ) are single operations on z.

Key takeaway

  • A complex number is a point (or arrow) on a plane: real part along one axis, imaginary part along the other.
  • Multiplication scales lengths and adds angles, so rotation becomes multiplication.
  • That makes AC circuit analysis, rotations, frequency analysis and curve drawing shorter and cleaner.

item.title: Weighted Average Explained with Examples
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Starting with the simple mean

Let’s consider this data:

2, 4, 6

The arithmetic mean is 4, since (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4. Here every value counts equally.

When values are not equally important

Now let’s say these are marks given by three judges to a participant in a competition. The first judge is more experienced, so whatever that judge gives should carry more weight. We multiply each mark by a weight:

Judge Mark () Weight ()
1 2 2
2 4 1.5
3 6 1

The average now tilts toward the marks with more weight. Like a hammer, more weight on one side shifts the centre of gravity.

The formula

The weighted average is the sum of each value times its weight, divided by the sum of the weights:

Dividing by the total weight keeps the result on the same scale as the data. If all weights are equal, it reduces to the ordinary mean.

Example 1: the judges

Judge Mark () Weight ()
1 2 2 4
2 4 1.5 6
3 6 1 6
Total 4.5 16

The weighted average (3.56) is lower than the simple mean (4), because the lowest mark came from the most trusted judge.

Example 2: course grades

A student scores 90 in Math (4 credits), 80 in English (3 credits) and 70 in Art (2 credits). The simple mean is 80, but a 4-credit course should count more than a 2-credit one.

Course Score () Credits ()
Math 90 4 360
English 80 3 240
Art 70 2 140
Total 9 740

The weighted average is higher than the simple mean, since the best score sits in the heaviest course.

Note

Weights need not add up to 1 or 100. Dividing by takes care of that. If they do sum to 1 (for example 0.5, 0.3, 0.2), the denominator is 1 and the average is just .

Key takeaway

  • Use the simple mean when every value is equally important.
  • Use a weighted average when some values matter more (expert judges, credit hours, group sizes).
  • The result always lies between the smallest and largest value, pulled toward the heaviest weights.

item.title: The Law of Large Numbers: What It Is and What It Is Not
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
What it says

The law of large numbers (LLN) says that as we collect more independent observations from the same distribution, the sample mean gets closer to the true mean:

For a fair coin, let for heads and for tails. Then , and the proportion of heads should approach 0.5 as we flip more.

Seeing it in R

Let’s flip a fair coin 10,000 times and look at the running proportion of heads.

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
n <- 10000
flips <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
running <- cumsum(flips) / seq_len(n)

df <- data.frame(n = seq_len(n), prop = running)

ggplot(df, aes(n, prop)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of flips (log scale)", y = "Proportion of heads")

The values at a few sample sizes:

      n heads proportion
1    10     8     0.8000
2   100    55     0.5500
3  1000   473     0.4730
4 10000  4999     0.4999

With 10 flips the proportion is far from 0.5; with 10,000 it is very close.

What it is not

1. It is not the gambler’s fallacy

After five heads in a row, tails is not “due”. The coin has no memory, and the next flip is still 50/50. The LLN does not say the past is corrected; it says the early streak gets diluted by the many flips that follow.

2. It does not say counts even out

The proportion approaches 0.5, but the difference between heads and tails does not shrink. It typically grows, like . Let’s check by repeating the experiment 5,000 times for each :

set.seed(1)
sizes <- c(100, 10000, 1000000)
sapply(sizes, function(n) {
  heads <- rbinom(5000, n, 0.5)
  mean(abs(2 * heads - n))
})
      n avg_abs_diff avg_prop_off
1 1e+02          8.0      0.07991
2 1e+04         78.2      0.00782
3 1e+06        794.8      0.00079

The gap between heads and tails grows from about 8 to about 800, yet as a share of the flips it shrinks toward 0.

3. It is not a promise for small samples

The LLN is a statement about the long run. Ten flips can easily give 8 heads, as in our simulation. Believing that small samples must look like the population is sometimes called the “law of small numbers”, and it is a mistake.

4. It does not make a single outcome predictable

The LLN describes averages over many trials, not the next trial. A casino cannot predict one spin, but it can predict its profit over a million spins.

5. It does not always apply

The LLN needs conditions. The observations should be independent (or weakly dependent) draws from the same distribution, and that distribution must have a finite mean. The Cauchy distribution has no mean, so its sample average never settles, however large is.

Note

Don’t confuse the LLN with the central limit theorem. The LLN says the sample mean approaches . The CLT describes the shape of the fluctuations around : roughly normal, with spread .

A limit that is not the law of large numbers

Not every “settles toward 0.5” story is the LLN. Let’s pick a number uniformly from with odd, and ask for the probability that it exceeds the mean. The mean is , so exactly of the values lie above it:

3 5 11 101 1001
0.3333 0.4000 0.4545 0.4950 0.4995

The values creep toward 0.5, but there is no randomness in this table. Each entry is an exact number from algebra, and the limit is the ordinary limit of a sequence.

This example Law of large numbers
What changes with the distribution itself (more points) the number of repeated trials of one fixed experiment
Randomness none; exact fixed numbers each trial is random, so the running average bounces at first
Type of convergence deterministic limit of a sequence of probabilities the random sample mean approaches
Guarantee follows from the formula random fluctuations average out over many trials

If anything, this example is closer to convergence in distribution: a discrete uniform distribution on points, rescaled to , approaches the continuous uniform distribution as . The LLN is about something else, namely random sample averages.

Key takeaway

  • Large samples give reliable averages, which is why surveys, trials and insurers work.
  • The coin never “evens things out”; a larger sample just dilutes early luck.
  • The LLN is about the average of many trials, not the next one.

item.title: When Is the Median a Good Measure of Center?
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
The median is the best measure of center when the data is lopsided, contains extreme values, or lacks exact numerical spacing. It simply picks the middle value after sorting, so extreme numbers at either end cannot pull it off-center.

Let’s go through the cases where the median outperforms the mean, each with a small example and its interpretation.

1. Skewed data

When most values cluster on one side and a few stretch into a long tail, the mean is dragged toward the tail. The median stays in the bulk of the data.

Example: prices (in thousands of dollars) of five homes sold in a neighbourhood:

250, 290, 310, 350, 4000

Interpretation: the median is 310, meaning half the homes sold for less and half for more. This is what a typical buyer pays. The mean is 1040, inflated by the single $4 million mansion, and no home in the list is anywhere near that price. The same applies to household income.

2. Severe outliers

Outliers come from rare events or measurement errors. One of them can ruin the mean, while the median barely moves.

Example: page load times in seconds for five visitors, one on a terrible connection:

1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 45.0

Interpretation: the median is 1.3 seconds, which matches the normal user experience. The mean is 10.0 seconds, wrongly suggesting the site is slow for everyone.

3. Ordinal data (ranked categories)

Ordinal data has a clear order, but the distance between categories is unknown or unequal. Words cannot be added or divided, so the mean cannot be computed.

Example: satisfaction ratings from five customers:

Poor, Fair, Good, Good, Excellent

Interpretation: after sorting, “Good” sits in the middle. We can say the typical customer rated the service “Good” without assigning arbitrary numbers to the words.

4. Censored or open-ended data

Sometimes extreme values are grouped into brackets such as “100+” or “Under 18”, or observations are cut off by the end of a study. Without the exact end values, the true mean cannot be calculated.

Example: survival in a 5-year medical trial where 60% of patients are still alive at the end, recorded only as “5+ years”.

Interpretation: we do not know how long those patients will live, but more than half of them passed 5 years, so the median survival time is greater than 5 years.

5. Skewed count data

Real-world counts often pile up at zero with a few big spikes.

Example: emergency room visits in a year for seven people:

0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 14

Interpretation: the median is 0, so the typical person never visits the ER. The mean is about 2.4 visits, a figure that matches almost nobody in the group.

6. Time-to-event data

Waiting times, delivery durations and task times have a hard floor at zero but no upper limit, which creates a natural right skew.

Example: support ticket resolution times in hours, where one complex bug took two days:

1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 48

Interpretation: with six values the median is the average of the middle two, (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5 hours, a realistic expectation for customers. The mean is 10 hours, which overstates the typical delay.

Quick summary: mean vs median

Scenario Best choice Why
Symmetric data without outliers (e.g. adult heights) Mean Uses every value for maximum precision
Skewed data or extreme outliers (e.g. salaries, home prices) Median Ignores the tails and reflects the middle of the crowd
Ranked labels or open-ended brackets (e.g. survey ratings, “65+”) Median Needs only order, not exact numbers at the extremes
Tip

Reporting both is often wise. A large gap between the mean and the median is itself a sign of skewness or outliers.

item.title: 7 Amazing Results in Statistics
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Some results in statistics are beautiful because a short statement has surprisingly wide consequences. Here are seven of our favourites. For each, we give the idea, then the reason it is amazing.

1. Chebyshev’s Inequality

For any distribution with a finite mean and standard deviation, at least of the data lie within standard deviations of the mean. So at least 75% lie within 2 standard deviations, and at least 88.9% within 3.

Why it is amazing: it needs no assumption about the shape. It is a safety net for skewed, heavy-tailed and U-shaped data alike. We look at it in detail in Why Chebyshev’s Inequality Is Great.

2. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

Take many random samples of the same size and compute each sample mean. As the sample size grows, the distribution of those means approaches a Normal (bell) curve, centred at the population mean, with spread .

Why it is amazing: it does not matter whether the original data are skewed, lumpy or discrete. Averages tend to be bell-shaped, which is why the Normal distribution, confidence intervals and many hypothesis tests work so well in practice.

3. The Law of Large Numbers (LLN)

While the CLT describes the shape of sample averages, the Law of Large Numbers describes their destination. As we repeat a random experiment again and again, the sample average converges to the true expected value.

Why it is amazing: it turns chaos into predictability. A single roulette spin is unpredictable, yet a casino can forecast its profit margin over millions of bets with very little uncertainty.

4. Bayes’ Theorem

Bayes’ Theorem is the exact rule for updating a belief when new evidence arrives. It flips a conditional probability around, giving the probability of a hidden cause from an observed effect:

Why it is amazing: it mimics rational learning and powers spam filters, medical diagnosis and many AI methods. It also shows that extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence. Suppose a disease affects 1 person in 1,000, and a test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. If someone tests positive, how likely is it that they have the disease?

prevalence  <- 0.001
sensitivity <- 0.99   # P(positive | disease)
specificity <- 0.99   # P(negative | no disease)

p_positive <- sensitivity * prevalence + (1 - specificity) * (1 - prevalence)
p_disease_given_positive <- sensitivity * prevalence / p_positive
round(p_disease_given_positive, 3)
[1] 0.09

Only about 9% of positive results are true. Most positives are false, because the healthy people vastly outnumber the sick.

5. Jensen’s Inequality

For a convex function , the average of the outputs is at least the output of the average:

For a concave function, the inequality reverses.

Why it is amazing: it explains why volatility hurts long-term growth. If an investment gains 50% one year and loses 50% the next, the average return is 0%, yet the money is multiplied by , a 25% loss. Growth is multiplicative, and the logarithm is concave, so the average of the log-growth falls below the log of the average growth.

6. Markov’s Inequality

Markov’s Inequality is the simpler parent of Chebyshev’s. For a non-negative random variable and any , it bounds the chance of a large value using only the mean:

Why it is amazing: averages cannot hide a large crowd of extreme values. Knowing nothing else about a country’s incomes, Markov’s inequality guarantees that no more than of the population can earn 5 or more times the national average.

7. The Coupon Collector’s Problem (and Linearity of Expectation)

Linearity of Expectation says that

and it holds even when and are dependent. Using it, we can find how many random draws are needed to collect all distinct items: about .

Why it is amazing: it replaces tangled dependency arguments with simple addition. It also shows why the last missing item takes so long. The first item is certain, but when only one item is missing, each draw finds it with chance , so we expect draws for that item alone.

We can check the formula by simulation. Take distinct items and repeat the collection 10,000 times:

set.seed(123)
n <- 50

draws_to_complete <- function(n) {
  seen <- rep(FALSE, n)
  draws <- 0
  while (!all(seen)) {
    seen[sample.int(n, 1)] <- TRUE
    draws <- draws + 1
  }
  draws
}

sim <- replicate(10000, draws_to_complete(n))
c(simulated = mean(sim), formula = n * log(n) + 0.5772 * n)
simulated   formula 
 224.9978  224.4612

Summary Comparison

Result What we need to know What it guarantees
Chebyshev’s Inequality Finite mean and standard deviation At least of the data lie within standard deviations of the mean.
Central Limit Theorem Independent samples with finite variance Sample means become approximately Normal as the sample grows.
Law of Large Numbers Finite mean Sample averages converge to the true average.
Bayes’ Theorem Prior probability and test accuracy The exact updated probability after seeing new evidence.
Jensen’s Inequality Mean and curve direction (convex or concave) Applying a curve to a random variable shifts the average away from the curve of the average.
Markov’s Inequality Only a non-negative mean A hard ceiling on the share of extreme high values.
Linearity of Expectation Individual averages only Averages add up cleanly, even when events are tangled together.

item.title: Why Chebyshev’s Inequality Is Great: A Guarantee for Any Distribution
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Chebyshev’s inequality is great because it guarantees a minimum percentage of data within a certain number of standard deviations from the mean, regardless of the distribution’s shape. We do not need to assume the data follow a Normal bell curve, which makes it a universal safety net for unknown, skewed, or U-shaped datasets.

The Core Formula

For any distribution with a finite mean () and finite standard deviation (), the proportion of data within standard deviations of the mean () is at least

  • Within 2 standard deviations (): at least of the data.
  • Within 3 standard deviations (): at least of the data.

Example 1: Heavy-Tailed Data (Household Income)

Income data are skewed to the right because a few very high earners pull the tail far out, so a Normal distribution fits poorly.

Suppose a city reports a mean household income of with a standard deviation of . What is the minimum percentage of households earning between $30,000 and $90,000?

  1. Find . Both boundaries are $30,000 from the mean. Dividing by the standard deviation gives .
  2. Apply Chebyshev. .

Without seeing a single tax return, or knowing the shape of the income gap, we can guarantee that at least 75% of households earn between $30,000 and $90,000.

Example 2: Server Latency and SLA Guarantees

Software response times often follow irregular patterns with random spikes, yet companies must still sign strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

Suppose an API has a mean response time of ms and a standard deviation of ms. A client asks for the worst-case share of requests that take 160 ms or longer (or 40 ms or less).

  1. Find . 160 ms is 60 ms from the mean, and gives .
  2. Apply Chebyshev. At least of requests fall between 40 ms and 160 ms. Conversely, at most 11.1% fall outside this range.

Even if network traffic is erratic, the engineers can promise that no more than 11.1% of requests will breach the 160 ms limit (the bound counts both tails, so it is conservative for the slow side alone).

Chebyshev vs. the Normal Distribution

Distance from mean () Normal distribution (bell curve only) Chebyshev (any distribution)
1.5 86.6% at least 55.6%
2 95.4% at least 75.0%
3 99.7% at least 88.9%
4 99.99% at least 93.8%
Note

Chebyshev gives a very conservative lower bound. If we know the data are Normal, the Normal distribution gives much tighter estimates.

Testing It in R

Let’s test the inequality on three very different shapes: a Normal bell curve, a heavily right-skewed Exponential, and a polarised U-shaped Beta (see the U-shaped distribution post). For each, we compute the exact share of data within standard deviations of the mean. All three should stay above Chebyshev’s 75% minimum.

set.seed(123)
n <- 100000

# Three completely different distribution shapes
data_normal <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)          # bell-shaped
data_skewed <- rexp(n, rate = 0.1)                   # heavily right-skewed
data_ushape <- rbeta(n, shape1 = 0.5, shape2 = 0.5)  # U-shaped

# Actual % of data within k standard deviations of the mean
check_chebyshev <- function(data, k = 2) {
  mu <- mean(data)
  sigma <- sd(data)
  actual_prop <- mean(data >= mu - k * sigma & data <= mu + k * sigma)
  round(actual_prop * 100, 2)
}

cat("Chebyshev minimum guarantee (k = 2): 75.00%\n")
Chebyshev minimum guarantee (k = 2): 75.00%
cat("Normal distribution actual:        ", check_chebyshev(data_normal), "%\n")
Normal distribution actual:         95.46 %
cat("Right-skewed (Exponential) actual: ", check_chebyshev(data_skewed), "%\n")
Right-skewed (Exponential) actual:  95.08 %
cat("U-shaped (Beta) actual:            ", check_chebyshev(data_ushape), "%\n")
U-shaped (Beta) actual:             100 %

All three comfortably exceed 75%. The bound is a floor valid for every distribution, not a typical value, so real data usually sit well above it.

Visualizing the Bounds

Here are the boundaries drawn over the skewed data.

library(ggplot2)

mu_skew <- mean(data_skewed)
sd_skew <- sd(data_skewed)

ggplot(data.frame(x = data_skewed), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_skew, colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_skew + c(-2, 2) * sd_skew,
             colour = "red", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(title = "Chebyshev Bounds (k = 2) on Skewed Data",
       subtitle = "Blue: mean. Red dashed: mean ± 2 SD (about 95% of the data lie inside here)",
       x = "Value", y = "Count")

The lower boundary falls below zero, so only the upper line is visible, yet the guarantee still holds.

item.title: Count Cells with Partial Text Matches in Excel Using COUNTIF
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Sometimes we need to count cells that contain only part of a text, such as every product with “Apple” in its name. An exact COUNTIF can’t do that, but wildcards can. To count cells that contain a substring anywhere inside them, we put the asterisk (*) on both sides of the search text:

=COUNTIF(range, "*substring*")

For example, this formula counts every cell in A2:A10 that has “Apple” anywhere in its text (case-insensitive), so “Green Apple”, “Pineapple” and “Apple Pie” all count:

=COUNTIF(A2:A10, "*Apple*")

Using a Cell Reference as the Search Term

If the search text lives in another cell (say B2), we can’t just type *B2*, because Excel would treat that as literal characters. Instead, we concatenate the wildcards around the cell reference with the & operator:

=COUNTIF(A2:A10, "*" & B2 & "*")

This builds the pattern "*Apple*" at runtime from whatever is in B2, so changing B2 updates the count instantly.

Other Wildcard Patterns

Two wildcards do all the work:

  • * matches any number of characters (including none)
  • ? matches exactly one character

Here is how we combine them:

Starts with a text:

=COUNTIF(A2:A10, "Apple*")

Ends with a text:

=COUNTIF(A2:A10, "*Apple")

One unknown character, e.g. matches “Jan” and “Jun”:

=COUNTIF(A2:A10, "J?n")

The Same Three Patterns with a Reference Cell

Suppose the search term is in A3 and the data sits in F9:F100. The row is locked with $ so the range stays put when we drag the formula down.

Contains (anywhere):

=COUNTIF(F$9:F$100, "*" & A3 & "*")

Starts with:

=COUNTIF(F$9:F$100, A3 & "*")

Ends with:

=COUNTIF(F$9:F$100, "*" & A3)
Note

In Google Sheets an open-ended range such as F$9:F also works. Excel needs an explicit end row (or a whole column like F:F).

TipHandle Empty Search Cells Safely

If A3 is blank, "*" & A3 & "*" becomes "**", which matches every text cell in the range. We can wrap the formula in an IF so it returns 0 when the criteria cell is empty:

=IF(A3="", 0, COUNTIF(F$9:F$100, "*" & A3 & "*"))

Testing A3="" is safer than ISBLANK(A3), because it also catches cells that hold an empty string returned by another formula.

Searching for a Literal * or ?

Since * and ? are wildcards, searching for them as ordinary characters needs a tilde (~) in front. This counts cells containing a real question mark:

=COUNTIF(A2:A10, "*~?*")

Quick Reference

  • COUNTIF is case-insensitive
  • Wildcards only match text; numbers stored as numbers are not counted by "*5*"
  • Use $ to lock the range (F$9:F$100) when dragging the formula down
  • For several conditions at once, use COUNTIFS with the same wildcard logic

Further Reading

  • Microsoft: COUNTIF function
  • Ablebits: COUNTIF with partial match

item.title: The Statistical Father: How a Bell Curve Settled Paternity Disputes
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
This post is an English retelling, with additions, of the Bengali article “পরিসংখ্যানিক পিতা!” by Dr. Rahmatullah Imon, shared on the earlier Stat Mania blog with his permission. The case details and the study figures below come from Dr. Imon’s account unless another source is named.

Before DNA tests existed, a court that doubted a child’s father had very little to go on. One of the most striking answers came from statistics: if a pregnancy lasted too long, the husband could not be the father. But how long is too long? A bell curve helped answer that.

A Baby Born 349 Days Later

In the late 1940s a British soldier, Major Hadlum, returned from the war to find that his wife had given birth to a child. Counting from the day he left, the baby arrived 349 days later. A normal pregnancy lasts about 280 days (40 weeks), so Hadlum suspected his wife had been unfaithful and petitioned for divorce on that ground.

The court held that such a long pregnancy was unusual but possible, so adultery was not proven. This was Hadlum v Hadlum, decided in 1948 and upheld on appeal in 1949.

Why a Single Number Is Not Enough

Other cases followed with gaps of around 340 and 360 days, and the judges had no agreed way to decide them. “Impossible” is a strong word for a biological process, since gestation length varies from one pregnancy to the next. What the courts needed was a cut-off, a point beyond which an outcome is so unlikely that we treat it as an outlier.

The Bell Curve Draws the Line

Gestation length is well described by a normal distribution centred near 280 days. The empirical rule says that about 99.7% of values lie within three standard deviations of the mean. Dr. Imon reports a large British study of more than 13,000 pregnancies that supported this shape, and that applying “mean + 3 SD” put the upper limit at roughly 360 days. (We could not independently confirm the details of that study, so treat its numbers as Dr. Imon’s account.)

Working backwards from the 360-day limit gives a standard deviation of about 27 days. We can check the arithmetic in R:

m <- 280
s <- 80 / 3                      # (360 - 280) / 3, about 26.7 days

pnorm(c(349, 360), m, s, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.00483 0.00135

So under this model, only about 0.5% of pregnancies run past 349 days, and about 0.14% past 360. Hadlum’s case sat at 2.6 standard deviations above the mean, rare but not impossible, while 360 days sits exactly at 3.

Note

The model is a simplification. Modern studies find that natural gestation varies more widely than the 280-day textbook figure suggests, and the distribution is not perfectly symmetric. The curve above is illustrative, not a medical reference.

The Court Draws a Line

In Preston-Jones v Preston-Jones, a husband had been abroad for about six months, and his wife’s child was born roughly 360 days after the last time they could have met. The trial judge refused the divorce, but the House of Lords, in a decision of December 1950 (reported in 1951), directed that the husband’s petition be allowed. One judge in the case had argued that a court should not accept such a pregnancy as possible without direct medical evidence.

It is common to read this as a rule that any child born within 360 days must be the husband’s. That is a simplification: the Lords decided one case on its evidence, and the 360-day figure became a practical benchmark rather than a statute. Even so, the idea behind it is a lesson in statistics. A “three-sigma” limit turned a vague legal question into a measurable one, and fathers in such cases were sometimes called “statistical fathers”.

What We Can Take from This

  • Outliers are judged against a distribution. A value of 349 days means little until we know the mean and spread of the data.
  • The three-sigma rule is a convention. Moving the cut-off to 2.5 or 4 standard deviations changes who is classed as an outlier.
  • Rare is not impossible. A statistical limit measures how surprising a value is, which is different from proving what happened in one real case.

References and Further Reading

  • Imon, R. (2017). পরিসংখ্যানিক পিতা! (Statistical Father!). Stat Mania (Bengali), 16 September 2017. The main source for this post.
  • McKenzie, D. (2014). Statistical outliers: of baldness and long gestations. Discusses Hadlum v Hadlum and the 360-day limit.
  • Preston-Jones v Preston-Jones, House of Lords, 14 December 1950; reported at [1951] AC 391.

item.title: Area Charts in Statistics: Probability, Proportions and Cumulative Totals
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
An area chart fills the space under a line with colour. That emphasises the volume or magnitude of the data, not only the change from one point to the next. Statisticians use area charts for three main jobs: showing probability, showing proportions of a total, and showing cumulative totals. Let’s see each, with R.

1. Probability and Continuous Distributions

For a continuous random variable, the area under the density curve is probability, and the total area is (or ). Shading a region turns an abstract idea into something we can see.

  • P-values and significance. Shading the tails of a distribution shows the rejection region for a significance level .
  • Confidence and coverage. Shading the middle of a curve shows how much probability lies in an interval, such as the , and zones of the Empirical Rule.

Here is the two-sided rejection region of a standard normal test at . The critical values are .

library(tidyverse)

z <- tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800), density = dnorm(x))
crit <- qnorm(0.975)   # 1.96

ggplot(z, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_area(data = filter(z, x <= -crit), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_area(data = filter(z, x >= crit),  fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Rejection region at alpha = 0.05 (shaded red)",
       x = "z", y = "Density")
# area in the two tails
2 * pnorm(-crit)
[1] 0.05

The two red tails together have area , which is the probability of a “significant” result when the null hypothesis is true.

2. Parts of a Total over Time: Stacked Area Charts

When a whole is made of several groups, a stacked area chart shows each group’s trend and the total at once. The top edge is the total, and the thickness of each band is that group’s contribution.

For example, here are made-up yearly emissions of a factory, split by pollutant.

set.seed(7)
emissions <- expand_grid(year = 2015:2025, pollutant = c("CO2", "NOx", "SO2")) %>%
  mutate(level = case_when(pollutant == "CO2" ~ 60, pollutant == "NOx" ~ 25, TRUE ~ 15) *
                 (1 - 0.02 * (year - 2015)) * runif(n(), 0.95, 1.05))

ggplot(emissions, aes(year, level, fill = pollutant)) +
  geom_area() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2025, 2)) +
  labs(title = "Factory emissions by pollutant (made-up data)",
       x = NULL, y = "Emissions (tonnes)", fill = NULL)

The total falls over the decade, and we can also see that CO2 is by far the largest part. A stacked area chart is best when the group order is fixed and the number of groups is small.

3. Cumulative Totals over Time

A line chart can hide the physical weight of accumulation. If the quantity adds up, such as rainfall during a season or the total number of cases in an outbreak, an area under the cumulative curve shows how much has built up.

set.seed(3)
rain <- tibble(day = 1:90, mm = rgamma(90, shape = 0.4, scale = 8)) %>%
  mutate(total = cumsum(mm))

ggplot(rain, aes(day, total)) +
  geom_area(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  labs(title = "Accumulated rainfall over a 90-day season (simulated)",
       x = "Day", y = "Total rainfall (mm)")

Overlapping Areas: Use Transparency

Areas that are not stacked need care. If we draw two independent groups on the same axes with solid fills, the one drawn later hides part of the other (occlusion), and the chart misleads.

Transparency solves this for a few series. With a semi-transparent fill (alpha around 0.4), both areas stay visible, and the overlap shows as a darker blend. The panels below show the same data three ways: solid fills, transparent fills, and lines.

set.seed(11)
two <- tibble(x = rep(1:30, 2), group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 30)) %>%
  mutate(y = 50 + cumsum(rnorm(60, 0, 2)) + ifelse(group == "B", 8, 0))

solid <- ggplot(two, aes(x, y, fill = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Solid: B hides part of A", x = NULL, y = NULL)

transparent <- ggplot(two, aes(x, y, fill = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Transparent: both visible", x = NULL, y = NULL)

lines <- ggplot(two, aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Lines: clearest", x = NULL, y = NULL)

library(patchwork)
solid | transparent | lines

In the solid chart, group B is drawn on top and hides the lower part of group A, so we cannot tell where A’s area really starts or how the two compare. In the transparent chart, we can read both series, and the overlap is visible. A good habit is to add a line along the top edge of each area, so that each boundary stays crisp.

ggplot(two, aes(x, y, fill = group, colour = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "Transparent areas with outlines", x = NULL, y = NULL)

Transparency has limits. With three or more overlapping series, the blended colours become muddy and the overlaps are hard to decode. Then a line chart is the better choice.

Tip

Use an area chart when the filled amount itself means something: probability, a total or a cumulative quantity. For two overlapping series, make the fills transparent. If only the trend matters, or there are three or more unstacked series, use a line chart.

Summary

Use Chart What the area shows
Probability, p-values, intervals Area under a density curve Probability
Parts of a whole over time Stacked area Each group’s share and the total
Accumulation Cumulative area The total built up so far
Two overlapping series Transparent areas (with outlines) Each series, and where they overlap
Three or more separate series Not an area chart Use lines

item.title: When Are Bar Charts Useful? Six Cases with R Examples
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A bar chart maps each value to the length of a bar. Our eyes compare lengths very accurately, which is why bar charts are the safest choice whenever we compare quantities across distinct categories. Here are six situations where they work well, each drawn in R. The data are made up for illustration.

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

1. Comparing Categories (Nominal Data)

When categories have no natural order, we sort the bars by size so that the ranking is obvious. Typical uses are sales by product line or web traffic by referral source.

traffic <- tibble(
  source = c("Organic search", "Direct", "Social media", "Email", "Referral"),
  visits = c(5200, 3100, 2400, 1300, 900)
)

ggplot(traffic, aes(x = reorder(source, visits), y = visits)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Website visits by source", x = NULL, y = "Visits")

Pareto chart

A Pareto chart sorts the bars in descending order and adds a line with the cumulative percentage. It shows the “vital few” categories that cause most of an outcome, such as the common reasons for customer complaints.

complaints <- tibble(
  reason = c("Late delivery", "Damaged item", "Wrong item", "Billing error", "Rude staff", "Other"),
  n = c(120, 75, 40, 25, 15, 10)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  mutate(reason = fct_inorder(reason), cum_pct = cumsum(n) / sum(n) * 100)

total <- sum(complaints$n)

ggplot(complaints, aes(reason)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = n), fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = cum_pct * total / 100, group = 1), colour = "tomato", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cum_pct * total / 100), colour = "tomato", size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Complaints",
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / total * 100, name = "Cumulative %")) +
  labs(title = "Reasons for complaints (Pareto chart)", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))

The first two reasons already account for over half of all complaints (68%), so that is where to act first.

2. Ordered Categories (Ordinal Data)

When categories follow a natural order, the bars keep that order. Likert survey answers are the classic case. We must keep the order of the scale, not sort by size.

likert <- tibble(
  answer = factor(c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree"),
                  levels = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree")),
  n = c(12, 25, 38, 80, 45)
)

ggplot(likert, aes(answer, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Responses to a survey statement", x = NULL, y = "Respondents")

Income brackets (low, medium, high) or performance tiers work the same way.

3. Discrete Time Blocks

Line graphs suit measurements that flow continuously. When each value is a total for a block of time, such as monthly rainfall, quarterly earnings or daily steps, a bar chart is more honest: each bar is one block, and nothing is implied between them.

rain <- tibble(month = factor(month.abb, levels = month.abb),
               mm = c(8, 12, 30, 80, 190, 330, 360, 330, 250, 130, 20, 5))

ggplot(rain, aes(month, mm)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Monthly rainfall (made-up data)", x = NULL, y = "Rainfall (mm)")

Bars also suit a few time points, such as an indicator over 5 years, where a line over so few points looks sparse.

4. Parts of a Whole: Stacked Bars

To see the total and its parts, we can segment each bar. A stacked bar shows the totals. A 100% stacked bar shows the shares, whatever the totals.

energy <- expand_grid(country = c("A", "B", "C"), fuel = c("Coal", "Gas", "Solar")) %>%
  mutate(twh = c(60, 30, 10, 20, 50, 30, 10, 20, 70))

stacked <- ggplot(energy, aes(country, twh, fill = fuel)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Stacked: totals and parts", x = "Country", y = "Energy (TWh)", fill = NULL)

filled <- ggplot(energy, aes(country, twh, fill = fuel)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "100% stacked: shares", x = "Country", y = "Share", fill = NULL)

stacked | filled

A diverging stacked bar is a variant for survey scales. It centres the bars on the neutral answer, with negative answers to the left and positive ones to the right, so the net sentiment is visible at once.

5. Two Categorical Variables: Clustered Bars

To compare groups across a second variable, we put the bars side by side.

salary <- expand_grid(department = c("Sales", "IT", "HR"), status = c("Full-time", "Part-time")) %>%
  mutate(avg = c(52, 30, 61, 38, 48, 29))

ggplot(salary, aes(department, avg, fill = status)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Average salary by department and status",
       x = NULL, y = "Average salary (thousands)", fill = NULL)

6. Horizontal Bars

Rotating the chart by 90 degrees helps in two situations.

Long labels. Vertical bars force the labels to tilt, while horizontal bars keep them readable.

depts <- tibble(
  department = c("Department of Environmental Protection", "Department of Public Transport",
                 "Department of Health Services", "Department of Parks"),
  budget = c(42, 65, 90, 18)
)

ggplot(depts, aes(x = reorder(department, budget), y = budget)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Budget by department", x = NULL, y = "Budget (millions)")

Population pyramids. Two horizontal bar charts share a vertical age axis, with one group to the left and the other to the right.

pyramid <- expand_grid(age = c("0-14", "15-29", "30-44", "45-59", "60+"), sex = c("Male", "Female")) %>%
  mutate(pop = c(26, 24, 28, 27, 25, 25, 19, 20, 12, 15),
         pop = ifelse(sex == "Male", -pop, pop),
         age = factor(age, levels = c("0-14", "15-29", "30-44", "45-59", "60+")))

ggplot(pyramid, aes(age, pop, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = abs) +
  labs(title = "Population pyramid (made-up data)", x = "Age group", y = "Population (millions)", fill = NULL)

When to Choose a Bar Chart, and When Not To

Choose a bar chart if… Avoid a bar chart if…
The horizontal axis holds distinct groups, brackets or blocks of time The axis is a continuous scale (exact age, temperature, seconds): use a line plot or histogram
The goal is comparing exact differences in magnitude There are dozens of categories that clog the axis: use a sorted horizontal bar chart or a table
We want a chart that non-technical readers understand at once We want to show a distribution (spread, quartiles, outliers): use a box plot
Tip

Always start the value axis of a bar chart at zero. The bar’s length is the message, so a truncated axis exaggerates differences.

For a comparison with pie charts, see pie chart vs bar chart, and for choosing a chart by data type see choosing a chart by data type.

item.title: Choosing a Chart by Data Type: Categorical, Quantitative or Both
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
The right chart depends on the type of data in our variables. A wrong choice can distort a relationship, or show data in a way that makes no statistical sense, such as a line graph joining unrelated categories. Let’s go through the three cases and draw an example of each in R.

1. Categorical Data

Categorical (qualitative) data are labels or groups: gender, country, car model, satisfaction level. The usual goal is to compare counts or percentages across groups.

Chart Best for Example
Bar chart Comparing counts or percentages between separate groups Patients by blood type (, , , )
Stacked or grouped bar A main category split by a second one Agree / disagree answers by age group
Pie or donut chart Parts of a whole, with at most about five categories Market share of a few firms
Pareto chart Finding the few most frequent categories to prioritise Frequency of manufacturing defects

2. Quantitative Data

Quantitative (numerical) data are measurable quantities for which arithmetic makes sense. They are either discrete (countable, like shoe sizes or the number of children) or continuous (any value in a range, like height, time or weight).

Chart Best for Example
Histogram The distribution, spread and skewness of one continuous variable Household incomes in a city
Density or area chart A smooth distribution, or tail regions A normal curve and its critical region
Box plot Five-number summary and outliers Exam scores in one school
Line graph A change or trend over time Global temperature from 1880 to today
Scatter plot The relationship between two quantitative variables Hours studied and exam score

3. Mixed Data: Categorical and Quantitative

To see how a number behaves across groups, we use charts that combine both types:

  • Side-by-side box plots are the standard way to compare a quantitative variable across categories, for example salary across job titles.
  • Faceted histograms show a small histogram for each category, so that we can compare shape, centre and spread.

One Example of Each in R

We use the mpg data set that ships with ggplot2 (fuel economy of 234 cars). Each panel matches a row of the tables above. The plots use the default grey panel.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

bar <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = reorder(class, class, length))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Categorical: bar chart", x = NULL, y = "Number of cars")

hist <- ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Quantitative: histogram", x = "Highway mpg", y = "Number of cars")

scatter <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Two numbers: scatter", x = "Engine size (litres)", y = "Highway mpg")

line <- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy / 1000)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Over time: line graph", x = NULL, y = "Unemployed (millions)")

box <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = reorder(drv, hwy, median), y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Mixed: box plot by group", x = "Drive type", y = "Highway mpg")

facet <- ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ drv, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Mixed: faceted histograms", x = "Highway mpg", y = "Cars")

(bar | hist | scatter) / (line | box | facet)

Notice what each chart answers. The bar chart ranks the categories, the histogram shows the shape of one variable, and the scatter plot shows how two variables move together. The line graph follows a change over time, while the box plot and the faceted histograms compare a number across groups.

Common Mistakes

  • A line graph for unordered categories. A line suggests a trend between points, so use bars for categories.
  • A pie chart with many slices. See pie chart vs bar chart and pie charts with many categories.
  • A histogram for categories, or a bar chart for a continuous variable. A histogram’s bars touch because the intervals are continuous, while the bars of a bar chart are separate.
Tip

Ask two questions first: what type is each variable, and what do we want to show (compare, see a distribution, follow a trend, or relate two variables)? The answers almost always point to one chart from the tables above.

Summary

We have We want Use
One categorical variable Compare counts Bar chart
One categorical variable Parts of a whole Pie or donut (few categories)
One quantitative variable See its distribution Histogram or box plot
Two quantitative variables See a relationship Scatter plot
A quantitative variable over time See a trend Line graph
Quantitative by categorical Compare groups Side-by-side box plots or faceted histograms

item.title: Can a Discrete Variable Have Fractional Values? Examples
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Many people think that a discrete variable must be a whole number, like the number of children. That is not the definition. A variable is discrete if it takes distinct, isolated values that can be counted, so that there is a gap between any two neighbouring allowed values. Those values may well be fractions or decimals.

What matters is not whether the numbers are whole, but whether values between two neighbours are possible.

Examples of Discrete Variables with Fractional Values

  • Shoe sizes. We can buy size 8, 8.5, 9 or 9.5, in steps of 0.5. A size 8.23 does not exist, so the set of values is separate and countable.
  • Stock prices before decimalisation. Before 2001, US stock exchanges quoted prices in fractions such as or of a dollar (for example or ). A price between two fractions was not allowed.
  • Pre-decimal British money. Before 1971, coins included the halfpenny (d) and the farthing (d). Prices moved in these fixed fractional steps.
  • Measuring cups. A standard set has , , and 1 cup. The capacity we can measure with one cup jumps from one of these fractions to the next.
  • Proportions with a fixed denominator. If we flip a coin 4 times, the proportion of heads can only be , , , or . A value like is impossible, because the denominator is fixed by .

Seeing the Last Example in R

For 4 coin flips, the number of heads follows a binomial distribution. Here are the probabilities of each possible proportion. The bars are separated, with nothing in between.

library(ggplot2)

flips <- data.frame(heads = 0:4)
flips$proportion <- flips$heads / 4
flips$probability <- dbinom(flips$heads, size = 4, prob = 0.5)
flips
  heads proportion probability
1     0       0.00      0.0625
2     1       0.25      0.2500
3     2       0.50      0.3750
4     3       0.75      0.2500
5     4       1.00      0.0625
ggplot(flips, aes(proportion, probability)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.05, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = flips$proportion, limits = c(-0.1, 1.1)) +
  labs(title = "Proportion of heads in 4 flips (discrete)",
       x = "Proportion of heads", y = "Probability")

Only five proportions can occur. If we had measured something continuous, such as the exact height of 4 people, any value in a range would be possible and the bars would merge into a curve.

Discrete or Continuous?

A useful test: can we always find another possible value between two given values? If yes, the variable is continuous. If no, it is discrete.

Variable type Value examples Countable and isolated?
Discrete (whole numbers) 1 child, 2 cars, 3 books Yes
Discrete (fractional) Size 7.5, size 8, size 8.5 Yes
Continuous 7.523 inches, 8.114 seconds No: infinitely many values between any two
Note

Measurements are often recorded in a discrete way. A person’s height is continuous, but when we write it to the nearest centimetre, the recorded values are discrete. It is the variable itself, not its rounding, that decides the type, so we classify height as continuous.

Summary

  • A discrete variable has separate, countable values with gaps between them.
  • Discrete does not mean whole numbers: shoe sizes, old stock prices and proportions of trials are all discrete fractions.
  • A variable is continuous when any value in a range is possible, with no gaps.

item.title: Is the Poisson Distribution Memoryless? Poisson vs Exponential
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A waiting time is memoryless if how long we have already waited tells us nothing about how much longer we will wait. Think of waiting for a random event, such as a call or a bus: after 20 minutes of waiting, we are no closer to the event than when we started. Does the Poisson distribution have this property?

Strictly speaking, the Poisson distribution itself is not memoryless. What is memoryless is the exponential distribution of the waiting time between events in a Poisson process. The two are closely linked, which is why they get confused. Let’s separate them.

What the Memoryless Property Means

A waiting time is memoryless if the past does not change the chance of a future outcome:

  • is the time we have already waited.
  • is the additional time we are asking about.

In plain words: if we have waited minutes and nothing has happened, the probability of waiting at least more minutes is exactly what it would be for someone who has just arrived. The process “forgets” how long it has run.

Poisson Count vs Exponential Waiting Time

Poisson Exponential
What it models The number of events in a fixed interval The waiting time between events
Type of variable Discrete (0, 1, 2, …) Continuous ()
Example Emails arriving in an hour Minutes between one email and the next
Memoryless? No Yes, and it is the only continuous distribution that is

The Poisson process has independent increments: counts in non-overlapping time windows do not affect each other. That is a different idea from memorylessness, which is a property of one waiting time.

If events arrive as a Poisson process with rate , the counts in a unit interval are Poisson(), and the waiting times between events are exponential with the same rate .

Checking the Memoryless Property in R

For an exponential waiting time, the probability of waiting longer than is . Let’s take a rate of events per minute (one event every 10 minutes on average), and ask: having waited minutes, what is the chance of waiting at least more?

rate <- 0.1
s <- 20
t <- 10

# P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > s + t) / P(X > s)
pexp(s + t, rate, lower.tail = FALSE) / pexp(s, rate, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.3678794
# P(X > t), for someone who has just arrived
pexp(t, rate, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.3678794

The two numbers are identical, . We can also check it by simulation, using only the waits that already exceeded :

set.seed(1)
waits <- rexp(1e6, rate)

mean(waits[waits > s] > s + t)   # among those who waited s, share who waited t more
[1] 0.3676605
mean(waits > t)                  # share of all waits longer than t
[1] 0.368468

Both are about , as the property says.

A Waiting Time That Is Not Memoryless

For contrast, think of a bus that comes on a timetable, every 30 minutes. If we arrive at a random moment, the wait is uniform from 0 to 30 minutes. Now the past matters.

library(tidyverse)

wait <- seq(0, 60, by = 0.5)
curves <- tibble(
  minutes = wait,
  Exponential = pexp(wait, 1 / 15, lower.tail = FALSE),
  Timetable   = punif(wait, 0, 30, lower.tail = FALSE)
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-minutes, names_to = "bus", values_to = "chance_still_waiting")

ggplot(curves, aes(minutes, chance_still_waiting, colour = bus)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Chance that we are still waiting after x minutes",
       x = "Minutes since we arrived", y = "Probability", colour = NULL)

For the timetable bus, once we have waited 20 minutes the bus is certain to come within 10 more. A new arrival could wait up to 30. The wait does depend on the past. For the exponential bus, the chance of waiting more minutes is the same no matter how long we have already waited.

Example: The Bus at a Random Stop

Suppose buses at a stop arrive at random, as a Poisson process, with per minute.

  • If we have already waited 20 minutes, the chance that we wait at least 10 more is .
  • A new passenger who has just walked up has exactly the same chance of waiting at least 10 minutes.
  • The bus does not become “due” because we have waited longer, and the process does not accumulate wear or memory.
Note

This is why waiting for a random event is frustrating. It is not that a long wait makes the event more likely. For truly random arrivals, the future is the same however long we have waited. A timetable is different, because there the past does carry information.

Summary

  • The Poisson distribution counts events in an interval, and is not memoryless.
  • The exponential distribution models the waiting time between those events, and is memoryless: .
  • It is the only continuous distribution with this property.
  • Related reading: Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used?

item.title: Multi-Line Comments in LaTeX: Three Ways to Comment Out a Block
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Plain LaTeX has only one kind of comment: everything after a % to the end of the line is ignored. To hide a whole paragraph, table or block of code, we have three options. Let’s look at each, and at when it can go wrong.

1. The Fastest Way: an Editor Shortcut

Select the block and press the editor’s comment shortcut. The editor puts a % in front of every selected line for us.

Editor Windows / Linux macOS
Overleaf, TeXstudio, VS Code, Texmaker Ctrl + / Cmd + /

The same shortcut removes the percent signs again. (Some editors use other keys: older TeXstudio versions use Ctrl + T to comment and Ctrl + U to uncomment. Check the editor’s menu if the shortcut does not work.)

This is the safest method, because the hidden lines are real comments. The cost is that the source now has a % on every line.

2. The Cleanest Way: the comment Package

The comment package gives us an environment that ignores everything inside it.

  1. Load the package in the preamble: \usepackage{comment}.
  2. Wrap the block in \begin{comment} and \end{comment}.
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{comment} % required in the preamble

\begin{document}

This text will be visible in the compiled PDF.

\begin{comment}
Everything written in this environment is completely ignored.
You can write several paragraphs, tables or code
without adding percent signs.
\end{comment}

This text will also be visible.

\end{document}

The PDF contains the first and the last paragraph only.

Note

The verbatim package also defines a comment environment, so \usepackage{verbatim} works in the same way. Some LaTeX installations load it already.

Warning

\end{comment} must be on a line of its own, with nothing else before or after it on that line.

3. The Package-Free Trick: \iffalse and \fi

Without any package, we can use a TeX conditional that is always false. TeX skips everything between \iffalse and \fi.

This text will print normally.

\iffalse
This is a multi-line comment.
LaTeX skips this whole section because the condition is false.
Change \iffalse to \iftrue to switch the block back on.
\fi

This text will also print normally.

This is handy for blocks we may want to bring back, since changing one word turns the block on again.

Warning

TeX still reads the skipped text to find the matching \fi. If the hidden block contains its own conditional, such as \ifnum or \ifx, then it must also contain the matching \fi. Otherwise LaTeX stops with “Incomplete \iffalse; all text was ignored”. Unknown commands and unmatched braces inside the block are fine.

A Switch for Draft Notes

The same idea gives a named switch, which is useful for notes that should appear only in a draft:

\newif\ifdraft
\draftfalse   % change to \drafttrue to show the draft notes

\ifdraft
Note to self: check this section before submitting.
\fi

Which Method Should We Use?

Method Needs a package? Best for
Editor shortcut No Quick debugging and ad-hoc hiding of lines
comment environment Yes (comment or verbatim) Clean, readable blocks and large sections
\iffalse … \fi No Package-free fixes and blocks we may switch back on

In short: use the shortcut for quick edits, the comment environment for large blocks we want to keep tidy, and \iffalse when we cannot add a package.

item.title: List Files by Last Modified Time in Linux with ls -lt
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Which file did we edit last? On Linux, the ls command can sort a folder by modification time. Let’s see the options, with real output from a small example folder.

The Basic Command

ls -lt
  • -l shows the long format: permissions, owner, size and date.
  • -t sorts by modification time, newest first.
total 20
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 20 17:20 script.R
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 15 08:45 data.csv
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 12 11:05 plot.png
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct  9 14:10 notes.md
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct  2 09:30 report.txt

Oldest First

Add -r to reverse the order:

ls -ltr
total 20
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct  2 09:30 report.txt
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct  9 14:10 notes.md
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 12 11:05 plot.png
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 15 08:45 data.csv
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 20 17:20 script.R

The newest file is now at the bottom, right above the prompt. This is handy in a long listing.

Only the Most Recent Files

To see just the newest few, pipe the listing to head:

ls -lt | head -n 3
total 20
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 20 17:20 script.R
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 Oct 15 08:45 data.csv

The first line of ls -l is the total line, so head -n 3 shows only two files. To see the newest five files, use head -n 6. Or drop -l and list names only, with no total line:

ls -t | head -n 5

A Clearer Date Format

By default ls shows the time for recent files and the year for old ones. For an unambiguous date and time, use the ISO style (GNU ls):

ls -lt --time-style=long-iso
total 20
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 2026-10-20 17:20 script.R
-rw-rw-r-- 1 abdullah abdullah 2 2026-10-15 08:45 data.csv

Other Timestamps

Every file has three timestamps. -t uses the modification time unless we ask for another one.

Timestamp Meaning Sort by it
mtime Last time the contents changed ls -lt
ctime Last time the file or its metadata (permissions, owner) changed ls -ltc
atime Last time the file was read ls -ltu
Warning

Be careful with -c and -u on their own. ls -lc only shows the ctime, but still sorts by name. We need -t as well, as in ls -ltc, to sort by that time.

For the exact timestamps of one file, use stat:

stat report.txt

Is It Different in the fish Shell?

The commands are the same. The sorting options belong to ls itself, not to the shell, and pipes work the same way, so ls -lt | head -n 6 runs unchanged in fish.

The one difference is that in fish, ls is a small wrapper function that adds colours and type indicators, and then calls the real ls. We can see it with type ls. To bypass the wrapper, use command ls.

fish also makes it easy to save a shortcut. This function lists the five newest files, and funcsave stores it permanently:

function lt
    ls -lt $argv | head -n 6
end
funcsave lt

After that, lt shows the newest files in the current folder, and lt ~/Documents shows them for another folder. A shorter alternative is an abbreviation, which expands as we type:

abbr -a lt 'ls -lt'

Quick Reference

Goal Command
Newest first ls -lt
Oldest first ls -ltr
Five newest files ls -lt \| head -n 6
Names of the five newest ls -t \| head -n 5
ISO dates ls -lt --time-style=long-iso
Sort by change time ls -ltc
Sort by access time ls -ltu

item.title: Normal Approximation to the Poisson Distribution (with R)
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A Poisson distribution can be approximated accurately by a normal distribution when the average rate is large. For small the Poisson is skewed to the right. As grows, the skew fades and the distribution becomes a symmetric bell. Let’s see when this works, how to use it, and how good it is. (For where the Poisson distribution comes from and what it is used for, see Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used?)

The Rule of Thumb

The approximation is reliable when:

  • for a rough, quick approximation, and
  • for good accuracy.

Matching the Parameters

A Poisson variable has mean and variance both equal to . We give the normal distribution the same mean and variance:

  • Mean:
  • Variance:
  • Standard deviation:

So, for large ,

The Continuity Correction

The Poisson counts whole numbers, but the normal distribution is continuous. To compensate, we move the boundary by , so that each whole number is represented by the interval from to .

Poisson probability Normal calculation

Example: Calls to a Call Centre

A call centre receives on average calls per hour. What is the probability of fewer than 20 calls in an hour?

Exact Poisson answer

“Fewer than 20” means :

Normal approximation

  1. Parameters: and .
  2. Continuity correction: becomes .
  3. Z-score:

  1. Table lookup: .

The approximation misses the exact value by only about .

Checking in R

# exact Poisson
ppois(19, lambda = 25)
[1] 0.1335748
# normal approximation, with continuity correction
pnorm(19.5, mean = 25, sd = 5)
[1] 0.1356661
# normal approximation, without the correction
pnorm(19, mean = 25, sd = 5)
[1] 0.1150697

Without the correction the answer is about , which is much farther from the exact . The correction is worth the extra half unit.

Watching the Poisson Become Normal

Let’s plot the Poisson probabilities (bars) for three values of , with the normal curve drawn over each.

library(tidyverse)

lambdas <- c(2, 7, 25)

# show each panel only over the range where the probability is not negligible
xrange <- function(l) c(max(0, l - 4 * sqrt(l) - 2), l + 4 * sqrt(l) + 2)

plot_data <- map_dfr(lambdas, function(l) {
  r <- xrange(l)
  tibble(lambda = l, x = ceiling(r[1]):floor(r[2]), poisson = dpois(x, l))
}) %>%
  mutate(label = factor(paste("lambda =", lambda), levels = paste("lambda =", lambdas)))

curve_data <- map_dfr(lambdas, function(l) {
  tibble(lambda = l, x = seq(xrange(l)[1], xrange(l)[2], length.out = 400),
         normal = dnorm(x, l, sqrt(l)))
}) %>%
  mutate(label = factor(paste("lambda =", lambda), levels = paste("lambda =", lambdas)))

ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = plot_data, aes(x, poisson), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x, normal), colour = "tomato", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Poisson (bars) and the normal curve N(λ, λ) (line)",
       x = "Number of events", y = "Probability")

What to look for:

  • : the peak is pressed against zero and the right tail is long. The normal curve even gives some probability to negative values, so it is a poor fit.
  • : the peak has moved away from zero and rounded off, but a slight skew to the right remains.
  • : the bars are centred and smooth, and the curve follows them closely.

How Good Is the Approximation?

One way to measure the error is the largest gap between the exact and approximate cumulative probabilities. We compare the normal approximation with and without the continuity correction.

max_error <- function(l, correction) {
  x <- 0:(3 * l + 10)
  shift <- if (correction) 0.5 else 0
  max(abs(ppois(x, l) - pnorm(x + shift, l, sqrt(l))))
}

tibble(lambda = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50)) %>%
  mutate(with_correction    = map_dbl(lambda, max_error, correction = TRUE),
         without_correction = map_dbl(lambda, max_error, correction = FALSE)) %>%
  mutate(across(-lambda, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable()
lambda with_correction without_correction
2 0.0442 0.1767
5 0.0290 0.1160
10 0.0207 0.0830
20 0.0148 0.0591
25 0.0132 0.0529
50 0.0094 0.0375

Two things stand out. The error shrinks as grows, and it is always much smaller with the continuity correction. At the largest error with the correction is about , which supports the rule of thumb of .

Tip

For a single probability, check the exact value with ppois() or dpois() when software is available. The normal approximation is mainly useful for hand calculation, and for seeing why the bell shape appears.

Summary

  • Use when is large, say (a rough check is ).
  • Always apply the continuity correction of .
  • The approximation improves steadily as grows.

Related: Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used? covers real-world uses of the Poisson distribution and the conditions under which it fits.

item.title: Visualizing the Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7) in R
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
The Empirical Rule, also called the 68-95-99.7 rule, tells us how data spread around the mean when the distribution is bell-shaped (normal). Let’s state it, check it with a simulation in R, and then draw it.

An Example First

Suppose the marks of a large group of students are bell-shaped, with a mean of and a standard deviation of . The Empirical Rule then says:

  • about of the students score within one standard deviation of the mean: between and ,
  • about score within two standard deviations: between and ,
  • about , almost everyone, score within three standard deviations: between and .

So a mark below or above is very unusual: fewer than students in .

The Empirical Rule

For a normally distributed data set with mean and standard deviation :

Range Share of the data
about
about
about

So nearly all the data lie within three standard deviations of the mean, and values further away are rare.

Checking the Rule with Simulated Data

Let’s simulate exam marks like these, with mean and standard deviation , and measure the share of marks within one, two and three standard deviations.

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)
scores <- rnorm(n = 10000, mean = 70, sd = 5)

mean_val <- mean(scores)
sd_val   <- sd(scores)

within <- function(k) mean(scores >= mean_val - k * sd_val &
                           scores <= mean_val + k * sd_val) * 100

tibble(sd_range = c("1 SD", "2 SD", "3 SD"),
       simulated = round(map_dbl(1:3, within), 2),
       theory    = round((pnorm(1:3) - pnorm(-(1:3))) * 100, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable()
sd_range simulated theory
1 SD 68.29 68.27
2 SD 95.53 95.45
3 SD 99.73 99.73

The simulated percentages are very close to the theoretical ones. The theory column is exact: , and . The familiar , and are rounded versions of these.

Visualizing the Results

First, the histogram of the scores, with lines at one, two and three standard deviations from the mean.
